hook.text: A self-driving car is a computer on wheels—and computers can be hacked.

buildup.text: Researchers have remotely hacked car brakes, steering, and acceleration in controlled demos.

discovery.text: A compromised fleet could be turned into weapons—thousands of cars steered off the road at once.

twist.text: Adversarial stickers on stop signs have fooled AI vision systems into reading them as speed limit signs.

climax.text: The industry is racing to build unhackable systems, but no connected device has ever been truly secure.

punchline.text: Making a car smart also makes it a target.

quiz.question: How have researchers tricked self-driving AI vision systems?
options: By painting roads a different color
By placing adversarial stickers on signs

details.summary: Self-driving cars are computers on wheels, making them vulnerable to hacking that could manipulate steering, braking, or navigation. Securing these systems against cyberattacks is a critical unsolved challenge.
details.whyItMatters: A hacked autonomous vehicle could become a weapon. As cars become more connected and autonomous, cybersecurity becomes a life-safety issue, not just a data privacy concern.
takeaways: Connected vehicles have dozens of potential attack surfaces
Researchers have demonstrated remote takeover of vehicle systems
Automotive cybersecurity standards like ISO 21434 are still maturing

faq.question: Has anyone actually hacked a self-driving car?
faq.answer: Security researchers have demonstrated remote access to vehicle systems, including steering and braking, on connected cars. No mass attacks have occurred yet, but the theoretical vulnerability has been proven repeatedly.

faq.question: How are manufacturers protecting against car hacking?
faq.answer: Automakers use encrypted communications, intrusion detection systems, over-the-air security updates, and network segmentation to isolate critical driving systems from entertainment and connectivity features.
